title: CUET PG Geophysics Chapter Sessions
note: Questions are transcribed from the user-uploaded study pages. Explanations are original instructional explanations added for study.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Classical Mechanics
chapters.description: 100-question guided chapter session covering Galilean invariance, frames, equivalence principle, planetary motion, fictitious forces, orbital mechanics and relativity foundations.

questions.question: Under a Galilean transformation x' = x − vt, t' = t, which quantity is not invariant?
questions.explanation: Velocity changes between inertial frames according to v' = v − V, so it is not invariant. Acceleration, mass, and the Newtonian force law are invariant under a Galilean transformation.

questions.question: The statement that the laws of mechanics are the same in all inertial frames is known as:
questions.explanation: Galilean relativity states that no inertial frame is physically preferred for the laws of Newtonian mechanics.

questions.question: If S' moves with constant velocity V relative to S, what is the Galilean velocity transformation?
questions.explanation: Differentiate x' = x − Vt with respect to t: v' = dx'/dt = v − V.

questions.question: If F = ma holds in inertial frame S, what is its form in another inertial frame S' moving at constant velocity relative to S?
questions.explanation: Because relative velocity is constant, a' = a. Thus the same force gives F' = ma' and the form of Newton's second law is unchanged.

questions.question: Maxwell's equations are not invariant under Galilean transformations. This inconsistency led to the development of:
questions.explanation: The conflict between Maxwellian electromagnetism and Galilean transformations motivated Einstein's special theory of relativity, which uses Lorentz transformations.

questions.question: Linear momentum is conserved for a closed system in an inertial frame. In another inertial frame S', what happens?
options: Total momentum changes by a constant amount
Neither momentum nor energy is conserved
questions.explanation: For a closed system, P' = P − MV_system. Since the relative velocity V is constant, the difference between frame momenta is constant; if dP/dt=0, then dP'/dt=0.

questions.question: In Galilean relativity, which quantity is considered absolute?
questions.explanation: Newtonian time is invariant: t'=t. Position, velocity and kinetic energy depend on the inertial frame.

questions.question: Which force is NOT Galilean invariant in the sense of having the same functional form under a Galilean transformation?
options: Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B)
A force depending only on relative distance
questions.explanation: The Lorentz force explicitly contains velocity and electromagnetic fields, whose transformation requires Lorentz rather than Galilean relativity. Conservative position-dependent forces retain their Newtonian form.

questions.question: A spaceship moves with constant velocity in space. An astronaut throws a ball. Which principle lets the astronaut predict the ball's trajectory relative to the ship without knowing the ship's constant velocity?
questions.explanation: All inertial frames are equivalent for Newtonian mechanics, so the constant translational velocity of the ship does not affect the internal equations of motion.

questions.question: Under a Galilean transformation, a particle of mass m has velocity v in S and S' moves with velocity V. What is ΔK = K' − K?
questions.explanation: Since v'=v−V, K'=½m(v−V)². Subtracting K=½mv² gives ΔK=−m v·V+½mV².

questions.question: A frame of reference is inertial if:
options: Newton's first law holds in it
It rotates with constant angular velocity
questions.explanation: An inertial frame is one in which a force-free body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity. Hence Newton's first law holds.

questions.question: An observer in a train accelerating with acceleration a0 observes a pendulum. What fictitious force acts on the bob?
questions.explanation: For a frame accelerating with a0 relative to an inertial frame, every mass experiences the fictitious translational force F_fict = −m a0. It acts opposite the frame's acceleration.

questions.question: The Coriolis force F_C = −2m(ω × v_r) is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air and fluids on a rotating Earth, influencing the sense of rotation of large-scale cyclones.

questions.question: The centrifugal force on a mass m at position r from a rotating frame's axis is:
questions.explanation: The centrifugal term is −m ω×(ω×r) when included in the rotating-frame fictitious-force expression; for perpendicular distance ρ from the axis its magnitude is mω²ρ outward.

questions.question: A reference frame attached to Earth is best described as:
options: A non-inertial frame primarily due to Earth's rotation
An inertial frame because its acceleration is negligible
A non-inertial frame primarily due to Earth's orbital motion
questions.explanation: Earth rotates, so a frame fixed to its surface is non-inertial and requires centrifugal and Coriolis terms. Its orbital acceleration also matters for some applications, but rotation is the standard reason.

questions.question: The Foucault pendulum provides experimental evidence for:
questions.explanation: The plane of a Foucault pendulum appears to rotate relative to Earth because Earth rotates beneath the pendulum's approximately fixed plane of oscillation.

questions.question: The Euler fictitious force in a rotating frame acts when:
options: The body moves relative to the frame
The frame's angular velocity is constant
The frame's angular velocity changes with time
The body is at the origin
questions.explanation: The Euler force is F_E = −m(dω/dt × r). It exists when the angular velocity of the reference frame changes.

questions.question: A river flows from north to south in the Northern Hemisphere. Due to the Coriolis effect, the water tends to erode which bank more?
questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere motion is deflected to the right. For southward motion, right is west, so the west bank experiences the greater tendency toward erosion.

questions.question: For a frame rotating with constant angular velocity ω about an inertial origin, the effective force on a particle is:
questions.explanation: The rotating-frame equation contains Coriolis and centrifugal terms. With constant ω, the Euler term vanishes: F_eff = F_true − 2mω×v' − mω×(ω×r').

questions.question: At Earth's equator, the Coriolis force is zero if the particle is moving:
questions.explanation: At the equator ω is horizontal and points along the Earth's rotation axis. For horizontal east-west motion, ω×v has zero magnitude because ω and v are parallel/antiparallel.

questions.question: The Weak Equivalence Principle states the equivalence between:
questions.explanation: The WEP states that the trajectory of free fall is independent of the composition or mass of the test body, corresponding to equality of inertial and gravitational mass.

questions.question: In Einstein's thought experiment, a closed windowless elevator cannot distinguish a uniform gravitational field from:
options: Uniform acceleration opposite to the gravitational field
questions.explanation: Einstein's equivalence principle says that locally, a uniformly accelerating frame can reproduce the effects of a uniform gravitational field.

questions.question: A direct consequence of the Principle of Equivalence is:
questions.explanation: The equivalence principle implies that gravity affects light through spacetime geometry. This leads to gravitational deflection/lensing of light near massive bodies.

questions.question: Gravitational redshift occurs because:
options: Photons gain energy leaving a gravitational well
Photons lose energy leaving a gravitational well
Time runs faster in stronger gravity
The speed of light changes locally
questions.explanation: A photon climbing out of a gravitational potential is observed at a lower frequency by a distant observer. In GR this is connected to gravitational time dilation.

questions.question: If inertial mass mi and gravitational mass mg were not equal, which observation would result?
options: Objects of different composition would fall with different accelerations
Speed of light would not be constant
questions.explanation: Free-fall acceleration is a = (mg/mi)g. If mg/mi differed between materials, different bodies would have different free-fall accelerations.

questions.question: Kepler's second law—equal areas in equal times—is a consequence of conservation of:
questions.explanation: Equal areal velocity follows from τ = dL/dt = 0 for a central force. Therefore angular momentum is conserved.

questions.question: For a particle of mass m and angular momentum L in a central potential U(r)=−k/r, the effective potential is:
questions.explanation: The radial motion can be written using U_eff(r)=U(r)+L²/(2mr²). The second term is the centrifugal barrier.

questions.question: For a stable circular orbit of radius r around a mass M, the orbital speed is:
questions.explanation: Set gravitational force equal to centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, giving v=√(GM/r).

questions.question: Escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R is:
options: Directly proportional to M and R
Proportional to √M and inversely proportional to √R
questions.explanation: v_e = √(2GM/R), so it scales as √M/√R.

questions.question: Tidal forces arise because the gravitational force exerted by one body on another is:
options: Not uniform across the diameter of the second body
questions.explanation: Gravity varies with position. The near side of an extended body feels a slightly different gravitational acceleration from the far side, producing tidal stretching.

questions.question: Galilean transformation equations rely on the assumption that:
options: Speed of light is the same in all frames
Time intervals are the same for all inertial frames
Clocks in moving frames run slow
questions.explanation: Newtonian mechanics assumes absolute time: t'=t. This is precisely what conflicts with special relativity at high speeds.

questions.question: An accelerated frame of reference is always:
options: A frame moving with constant velocity
questions.explanation: An accelerated frame does not satisfy Newton's first law without introducing fictitious forces; therefore it is non-inertial.

questions.question: A freely falling object observed from a freely falling elevator in a uniform gravitational field follows approximately:
options: A straight line with constant velocity
questions.explanation: Both the elevator and object have the same gravitational acceleration. Relative to the elevator, their relative acceleration is zero, so the object moves with constant velocity.

questions.question: Kepler's third law T² ∝ a³. If planet 1 is four times farther from the same star than planet 2, T1/T2 is:
A satellite is geostationary if:
options: Its orbital period is 24 h and it orbits in Earth's equatorial plane
It orbits from pole to pole
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite has the same angular velocity as Earth, a circular equatorial orbit, and the same direction of rotation, giving an approximately 24-hour period.

questions.question: The term L²/(2mr²) in the effective potential is often called:
questions.explanation: L²/(2mr²) is the effective centrifugal potential arising from angular momentum in radial motion.

questions.question: The total energy of a planet in an elliptical orbit around the Sun is:
questions.explanation: A bound Kepler orbit has E<0. The total mechanical energy remains constant even though kinetic and potential energies vary.

questions.question: The Strong Equivalence Principle differs from the Einstein Equivalence Principle because it applies to:
questions.explanation: SEP extends equivalence to local gravitational experiments and includes self-gravitating systems/gravitational binding energy, going beyond the EEP's non-gravitational local physics.

questions.question: A person on a weighing scale in an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a reads:
questions.explanation: The scale supplies the normal force N. For upward acceleration, N−mg=ma, so N=m(g+a).

questions.question: Which fictitious force is independent of the object's velocity relative to the non-inertial frame?
questions.explanation: Coriolis force is proportional to relative velocity, while centrifugal force depends on position and angular velocity, not relative velocity.

questions.question: Failure of Galilean transformations to leave the electromagnetic wave equation invariant implied that:
options: Either Galilean relativity or electromagnetism must fail at high speeds
A preferred ether frame must exist
Speed of light is not universal
questions.explanation: The Maxwell equations predict an invariant light speed, incompatible with Galilean velocity addition. Special relativity replaces Galilean transformations with Lorentz transformations.

questions.question: If F depends only on position relative to the origin, under what condition is the force Galilean invariant?
options: Only if the origin is invariant
questions.explanation: A force depending on absolute position relative to a fixed origin does not retain the same functional form under a Galilean boost, because r'=r−Vt. Only translationally invariant force laws based on relative coordinates retain the same form.

questions.question: Deflection of a long-range artillery shell from its intended path is an example of:
questions.explanation: The projectile moves relative to the rotating Earth, so the Coriolis force produces a lateral deflection.

questions.question: Lagrange points are positions in the restricted three-body problem where gravitational and rotating-frame effects balance. A small object can:
options: Fall immediately into the larger body
Remain fixed relative to the two large bodies
questions.explanation: At Lagrange points, the gravitational forces and centrifugal effect in the rotating frame balance so the small body can remain at a fixed location relative to the two massive bodies.

questions.question: A gravitational-assist or slingshot maneuver changes a spacecraft's velocity relative to the Sun by:
options: Exchanging momentum and kinetic energy with a moving planet
questions.explanation: In the planet's frame the hyperbolic flyby is approximately elastic, but the planet itself moves around the Sun, allowing the spacecraft to gain or lose heliocentric energy.

questions.question: According to the equivalence principle, gravity is locally indistinguishable from:
options: A fictitious force in an accelerated frame
questions.explanation: Locally, a uniform gravitational field and a uniformly accelerated reference frame produce equivalent effects on freely falling test bodies.

questions.question: In a non-inertial frame translating with acceleration a0, Newton's second law contains the fictitious force:
questions.explanation: A translationally accelerating frame introduces F_fict=−m a0, opposite the acceleration of the frame.

questions.question: An orbit with eccentricity e=1 is a:
questions.explanation: For Keplerian conics, e<1 is ellipse, e=1 parabola, and e>1 hyperbola. A parabola is the escape boundary with zero total energy.

questions.question: A clock at sea level compared with a clock on a high mountain runs, due to gravitational time dilation:
questions.explanation: The deeper gravitational potential at sea level makes the lower clock run more slowly relative to a clock higher in the gravitational field.

questions.question: Invariance of the laws of mechanics under Galilean transformations implies:
options: There is no absolute standard of rest
Mechanical experiments can determine absolute lab velocity
questions.explanation: No inertial frame is preferred by Newtonian mechanics; uniform motion cannot be detected by internal mechanical experiments.

questions.question: Earth is an oblate spheroid, bulged at the equator, primarily because of:
options: Centrifugal force due to Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: Rotation produces an outward centrifugal effect that is greatest at the equator, causing the rotating Earth to bulge there.

questions.question: Mercury's perihelion precession is not fully explained by Newtonian planetary perturbations. The remaining part is explained by:
questions.explanation: Einstein's general relativity predicts an additional advance of Mercury's perihelion due to spacetime curvature near the Sun.

questions.question: A particle dropped from height h at the equator is deflected by the Coriolis force toward the:
questions.explanation: A freely falling body gains an eastward component relative to the rotating Earth because it retains the larger eastward tangential speed it had at its higher latitude/radius. The standard result is an eastward deflection.

questions.question: The principle that the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of where and when it is performed is called:
questions.explanation: Local position invariance states that local non-gravitational experiment outcomes do not depend on location or time in the universe.

questions.question: If a particle has positive total energy E in a central 1/r potential, its trajectory is:
questions.explanation: For U=−k/r, E<0 gives bound ellipses, E=0 gives a parabola, and E>0 gives an unbound hyperbola.

questions.question: Acceleration is Galilean invariant because differentiating v'=v−V with respect to time gives:
questions.explanation: Since V is constant, dv'/dt=dv/dt. Thus acceleration is identical in all Galilean inertial frames.

questions.question: In the Southern Hemisphere, an object moving horizontally over Earth's surface is deflected to the:
questions.explanation: The Coriolis deflection is to the left of motion in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.question: Atmospheric drag on a low-Earth-orbit satellite causes its total mechanical energy to:
questions.explanation: Drag removes mechanical energy from the satellite. For a sequence of circular orbits, lower orbital radius means larger orbital speed, so the satellite's total mechanical energy decreases while its orbital speed increases.

questions.question: If gravity were suddenly turned off, an astronaut in a circular Earth orbit would:
options: Move along a straight line tangent to the original orbit
questions.explanation: Gravity provides the centripetal acceleration. Without it, Newton's first law makes the astronaut continue along the instantaneous tangent.

questions.question: For a simple pendulum in a non-inertial frame with effective acceleration g_eff, the small-angle equation is:
questions.explanation: The restoring torque is proportional to g_eff sinθ. Thus θ¨+(g_eff/l)sinθ=0; for small angles, θ¨+(g_eff/l)θ≈0.

questions.question: The work done by a central force over a closed orbital path is:
questions.explanation: A central gravitational force is conservative, so its work around any closed path is zero.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a fictitious force?
questions.explanation: Coriolis, centrifugal and Euler forces arise from non-inertial coordinates. Gravity is a physical interaction in Newtonian mechanics, not a fictitious force.

questions.question: A key feature of an inertial frame is that objects with no net force acting on them:
questions.explanation: Newton's first law states that a force-free body maintains constant velocity in an inertial frame.

questions.question: For U = −GMm/r, the negative sign indicates:
options: The force is attractive and U=0 at infinite separation
Potential energy is always negative in every system
questions.explanation: Choosing U=0 at infinity gives U<0 at finite r. The negative gradient produces an attractive force toward the mass.

questions.question: Two satellites A and B orbit a planet in circular orbits. If A has a greater orbital radius than B, which is true?
options: A has greater speed and longer period
A has smaller speed and shorter period
A has smaller speed and longer period
A has greater speed and shorter period
questions.explanation: v=√(GM/r) decreases with radius, while T=2π√(r³/GM) increases with radius.

questions.question: The principle of equivalence implies that light rays bend in a gravitational field. This effect is:
options: Twice the amount predicted by simple Newtonian corpuscular theory
Same as predicted by Newtonian corpuscular theory
questions.explanation: General relativity predicts a light-deflection angle that, in the weak-field solar-limb case, is twice the simple Newtonian corpuscular estimate.

questions.question: If energy is conserved in inertial frame S for a two-particle collision, what can be said about energy in another inertial frame S'?
options: Energy is conserved but its numerical value may differ
Energy is conserved only if collision is elastic
Energy is conserved only if total momentum is zero
questions.explanation: A Galilean boost changes kinetic energies by terms involving total momentum and V, so the numerical value changes, but if the isolated system's energy is conserved in one inertial frame, it is conserved in every inertial frame.

questions.question: At the North Pole, the plane of a Foucault pendulum appears to rotate:
questions.explanation: At the North Pole the Foucault precession period is 24 h. In the usual local/Northern-Hemisphere convention, the oscillation plane appears to rotate clockwise relative to the ground.

questions.question: For a circular orbit close to a planet's surface, escape velocity v_e and orbital velocity v_o satisfy:
questions.explanation: v_o=√(GM/R) while v_e=√(2GM/R), so v_e=√2 v_o.

questions.question: A car turns a corner at constant speed and a passenger feels pushed outward. This is due to:
options: Centrifugal force in the car's non-inertial frame
questions.explanation: The turning car is a rotating/non-inertial frame. The apparent outward centrifugal force is opposite the required inward centripetal acceleration.

questions.question: Why are 'fixed stars' often considered a good approximation of an inertial frame?
options: Their proper motions and accelerations are negligible because of their great distances
They are not subject to gravity
questions.explanation: Distant stars have small apparent angular accelerations and proper motions over laboratory timescales, providing an approximately inertial reference direction.

questions.question: The term 'pseudo-force' is another name for a fictitious force because:
options: It does not obey Newton's third-law action-reaction pairing in the same way as interaction forces
questions.explanation: Pseudo-forces are coordinate effects introduced in non-inertial frames. They are not produced by a physical interaction partner, so they do not form ordinary Newton-third-law pairs.

questions.question: The fact that all objects, regardless of mass or composition, fall with the same acceleration in vacuum is a direct experimental confirmation of:
questions.explanation: Universal free fall shows that gravitational acceleration is independent of the test body's composition, expressing the equality of inertial and gravitational response.

questions.question: Perturbations in Uranus's orbit led to the discovery of which planet?
questions.explanation: Unexplained deviations in Uranus's orbit were used by Adams and Le Verrier to predict the position of Neptune, which was subsequently observed.

questions.question: The magnitude of the Coriolis force is proportional to the object's speed relative to the rotating frame. For a stationary object in the rotating frame, the Coriolis force is:
questions.explanation: F_C=2mωv_rel sinθ. If v_rel=0, the Coriolis force is zero.

questions.question: Because F_C is proportional to ω×v_r, the Coriolis force is always perpendicular to:
options: Both angular velocity and relative velocity
questions.explanation: A cross product is perpendicular to each of its two vectors, so ω×v_r is perpendicular to both ω and v_r.

questions.question: A rocket is fired vertically upward. In the rocket's accelerating frame, the gravitational force appears to:
options: Decrease or even reverse depending on the acceleration
questions.explanation: The effective gravitational acceleration is g_eff=g−a for an upward-accelerating rocket. If a exceeds g, the effective direction reverses.

questions.question: The existence of Lagrange points is a consequence of the:
questions.explanation: Lagrange points arise in the restricted three-body problem: two massive bodies orbit their common centre and a negligible third body moves in their combined rotating gravitational field.

questions.question: For an object in a bound orbit under a central force, its total mechanical energy must be:
questions.explanation: For gravitationally bound Keplerian motion, E<0. Zero is the parabolic escape threshold and positive energy gives an unbound hyperbolic trajectory.

questions.question: Galilean invariance of Newton's second law requires that force be independent of:
options: Absolute velocity of the reference frame
questions.explanation: Under a Galilean boost, velocities change by a constant V but accelerations do not. A force law must therefore not depend on an absolute frame velocity.

questions.question: A child moves from the centre toward the edge of a merry-go-round rotating at constant angular velocity. The child experiences a Coriolis force directed:
questions.explanation: For outward radial velocity v_r and angular velocity ω, −2m(ω×v_r) points opposite the tangential direction of rotation.

questions.question: Eötvös-type tests of the Weak Equivalence Principle have confirmed equality of inertial and gravitational mass to approximately:
questions.explanation: High-precision equivalence-principle experiments constrain composition-dependent differences to extremely small levels, around the 10^−12 scale in the formulation used in the supplied question.

questions.question: A long-duration satellite trajectory is affected by Earth's non-spherical shape (equatorial bulge). This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Earth's gravitational potential is not exactly spherical. Higher multipole terms perturb an ideal Kepler orbit, producing effects such as nodal and apsidal precession.

questions.question: A particle moves in the xy-plane of a frame rotating with angular velocity ω=ω k. If v_r=v_x i, the Coriolis force is in the:
questions.explanation: ω×v = (ωk)×(v_x i)=ωv_x j. Since F_C=−2m(ω×v), it points in the −j direction.

questions.question: If a car suddenly stops, you lurch forward because:
options: A forward force acts on you
A fictitious force pushes you forward
Your inertia tends to keep you moving at the car's initial velocity
The Coriolis force acts on you
questions.explanation: Your body was moving with the car. When the car stops, your body tends to maintain its previous velocity due to inertia until another force changes it.

questions.question: The concept of an inertial frame is an idealization because:
options: No object in the universe is truly isolated from all forces
Every object accelerates relative to every other object
questions.explanation: Perfect isolation is an idealization. Real reference frames can be influenced by distant masses and rotations, so an exactly inertial frame is an approximation.

questions.question: A spring tide (larger-than-average tide) occurs when:
options: Sun and Moon are aligned with Earth at new or full moon
Sun and Moon are at right angles
A storm coincides with high tide
questions.explanation: At new and full moon, solar and lunar tidal forces reinforce each other, producing spring tides.

questions.question: In classical mechanics, space is Euclidean, homogeneous and isotropic. Homogeneity of space leads to conservation of:
questions.explanation: By Noether's theorem, continuous spatial translation symmetry (homogeneity) corresponds to conservation of linear momentum.

questions.question: Why do central forces such as gravity conserve angular momentum?
options: The force depends only on distance
Torque τ=r×F is zero because r and F are parallel or antiparallel
questions.explanation: For a central force F=F(r) r_hat, r and F are collinear, so τ=r×F=0 and dL/dt=0.

questions.question: If Earth's rotation speed increases, the apparent weight of a person at the equator would:
questions.explanation: At the equator the centrifugal acceleration ω²R increases with rotation rate. The normal force needed to support the person decreases: N=mg−mω²R.

questions.question: For a Foucault pendulum, the period of one full rotation is T=24 h/sinλ. At the equator λ=0, the period is:
options: Infinite; the plane does not rotate
questions.explanation: At λ=0, sinλ=0, so the precession angular rate is zero. The mathematical period tends to infinity: the oscillation plane does not rotate relative to Earth.

questions.question: General Relativity, built on the equivalence principle, describes gravity as:
options: A fictitious force in accelerated frames only
Curvature of spacetime caused by mass-energy
questions.explanation: Einstein's field equations relate spacetime curvature to stress-energy. Free bodies follow geodesics rather than being pulled by a Newtonian force in the fundamental description.

questions.question: A satellite in an elliptical orbit has its greatest speed at:
options: The point at the minor axis end
questions.explanation: Angular momentum conservation gives r v_t = constant, so tangential speed is greatest where r is smallest: at perigee.

questions.question: A frame S' accelerates relative to an inertial frame S. For a force-free particle, the observer in S' observes acceleration caused by:
options: A real force appearing only in S'
questions.explanation: In S the particle has zero acceleration. In S' the frame acceleration creates a fictitious force F_fict=−ma_frame, giving an apparent acceleration.

questions.question: For a system moving under a central inverse-square force, the virial theorem relates average kinetic and potential energies as:
questions.explanation: For a bound system with a 1/r potential, the virial theorem gives 2⟨T⟩=−⟨U⟩. Hence total energy ⟨E⟩=⟨T+U⟩=−⟨T⟩.

questions.question: For a geostationary satellite, the force providing the necessary centripetal acceleration is:
questions.explanation: In an inertial frame the required centripetal acceleration is supplied by Earth's gravity. The centrifugal force appears only when using the co-rotating frame.

questions.question: The transformation x' = x − ½at², y'=y, z'=z, t'=t represents a frame that is:
questions.explanation: The term −½at² is the displacement of a frame accelerating with constant acceleration a relative to S. Differentiating twice gives a' = a_particle − a_frame.

questions.question: An object weighed at the North Pole and then at the Equator has a slightly lower spring-balance reading at the Equator. Why?
options: Gravity is weaker at the Equator only
Centrifugal effect opposes gravity at the Equator
Coriolis force is zero at the Equator
questions.explanation: At the equator the centrifugal acceleration due to Earth's rotation is maximum and reduces the normal force required for support.

questions.question: The Principle of Equivalence 'erases' gravity locally. This means:
options: In a small enough freely falling region, gravitational effects can locally be transformed away
Gravity and electromagnetism are the same force
Inertial mass is only locally equal to gravitational mass
questions.explanation: A freely falling local inertial frame removes the uniform gravitational acceleration at that point. Tidal effects remain, so gravity cannot be globally eliminated.

questions.question: Galilean invariance is a limiting case of Lorentz invariance when:
options: Relative velocities are much smaller than the speed of light
questions.explanation: Lorentz transformations approach Galilean transformations when v/c≪1. Relativistic corrections then become negligible.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Conservation Laws in Mechanics
chapters.description: 12-question starter session covering momentum conservation, collisions, centre of mass, impulse and variable-mass systems.

questions.question: The law of conservation of linear momentum is a direct consequence of which Newtonian laws?
options: Newton's second and third laws combined
questions.explanation: For a closed system, the second law gives dP/dt equal to total external force, while Newton's third law makes internal action-reaction forces cancel in pairs. With no external force, total momentum is constant.

questions.question: A bomb of mass 3m at rest explodes into masses m and 2m. If the smaller mass moves with speed v, what is the total kinetic energy released?
questions.explanation: Initial momentum is zero, so m v = 2m u, giving u=v/2 for the 2m fragment. Total kinetic energy is ½mv² + ½(2m)(v/2)² = ¾mv².

questions.question: The principle of conservation of linear momentum is equivalent to the statement of:
questions.explanation: Spatial translation symmetry (homogeneity of space) leads to conservation of linear momentum through Noether's theorem.

questions.question: A body of mass m1 moving with velocity v1 makes a head-on elastic collision with a stationary mass m2. The velocity of m1 after collision is:
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum and kinetic energy for a one-dimensional elastic collision with u2=0 gives v1'=(m1−m2)/(m1+m2) v1.

questions.question: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the coefficient of restitution e is:
questions.explanation: In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together, so their relative separation speed after collision is zero. Hence e=0.

questions.question: A force F=(3t² i + 2t j) N acts on a particle. The change in linear momentum from t=1 s to t=2 s is:
questions.explanation: The momentum change is the impulse: Δp=∫Fdt. Integrating 3t² from 1 to 2 gives 7, while integrating 2 from 1 to 2 gives 2.

questions.question: The centre of mass of a system continues to move with uniform velocity if:
options: The sum of internal forces is zero
The sum of external forces is zero
The sum of torques is zero
questions.explanation: The centre-of-mass equation is M a_CM=F_ext,total. Therefore zero net external force gives constant centre-of-mass velocity.

questions.question: A man of mass 80 kg jumps from a stationary boat and moves at 2 m/s relative to the shore. The boat has mass 40 kg. The boat's speed is:
questions.explanation: Initial momentum is zero. Thus 80(2)+40v_boat=0, so v_boat=−4 m/s. The magnitude is 4 m/s, opposite the man's motion.

questions.question: If the total linear momentum of a system is conserved, which statement is always true?
options: Total kinetic energy is also conserved
Velocity of the centre of mass is constant
No work is done by any force
questions.explanation: P=Mv_CM. For a system with constant total mass, constant P implies constant centre-of-mass velocity, independent of whether kinetic energy is conserved.

questions.question: Two particles of masses m and 4m have the same kinetic energy. The ratio of their linear momenta is:
questions.explanation: For nonrelativistic particles p=√(2mK). With equal K, p is proportional to √m, so p_m:p_4m=√m:√(4m)=1:2.

questions.question: In the variable-mass equation F_ext + u(dm/dt) = m dv/dt, u represents:
options: Velocity of the ejected/accreted mass relative to the main body
Velocity of the main body relative to an inertial frame
Velocity of the ejected mass relative to the centre of mass
Velocity of the centre of mass
questions.explanation: The relative velocity u accounts for momentum carried into or out of the variable-mass body. Its sign convention must be consistent with the chosen dm/dt convention.

questions.question: A rocket ejects fuel at rate dm/dt=−λ with exhaust speed v_e relative to the rocket. The instantaneous thrust magnitude is:
questions.explanation: The thrust magnitude equals mass ejection rate times exhaust speed relative to the rocket: F_thrust=λv_e, with direction opposite to the exhaust flow.
